title: Endometriosis
summary: A presumptive clinical diagnosis based on symptoms and exam/imaging is now sufficient to start treatment, reserving surgery for refractory or fertility-related cases.
key_points: Suspect with dysmenorrhea, deep dyspareunia, dyschezia, dysuria, chronic pelvic pain, or infertility
Clinical diagnosis (history + exam +/- imaging) is sufficient to start empiric treatment; laparoscopy is not required first
Transvaginal ultrasound is first-line imaging; MRI or expert ultrasound if deep infiltrating disease suspected
ASRM revised staging (I-IV) scores implants, adhesions, and cul-de-sac obliteration
An endometrioma automatically makes the disease at least stage III; obliterated cul-de-sac is stage IV
Definitive diagnosis is histologic at surgery, but this is not a prerequisite for treating symptoms
Deep disease can involve bowel, bladder, or ureter — assess before planning surgery
management: First line: NSAIDs plus combined hormonal contraceptives or progestin-only therapy, started empirically
Second line for refractory pain: GnRH agonist or antagonist, with add-back therapy to limit bone/vasomotor effects
Conservative laparoscopic excision/ablation of lesions plus adhesiolysis for pain or fertility goals
For stage III/IV with infertility, surgery can improve spontaneous conception; repeat surgery rarely helps further
IVF is generally preferred over repeat surgery after an initial surgical attempt fails
No proven fertility benefit from hormonal therapy immediately before or after fertility-focused surgery
Hysterectomy (+/- oophorectomy) reserved as last resort for refractory disease after other options fail
citations: ACOG Clinical Practice Guideline No. 11, "Diagnosis of Endometriosis" (2026)
ASRM Practice Committee, endometriosis staging and surgical management guidance (current edition — verify at asrm.org)

title: Adnexal Mass Evaluation and Ovarian Cancer Risk Stratification
summary: Most adnexal masses are benign even after menopause; ultrasound morphology plus selective use of tumor markers and risk indices determines who needs gyn oncology referral.
key_points: Most adnexal masses, including in postmenopausal patients, are benign
Quality transvaginal ultrasound (accredited sonographer) is the primary imaging test
Simple cysts up to 10 cm can be followed with serial ultrasound rather than immediate surgery, even postmenopausally
CA-125 is more useful postmenopausally; premenopausally it is nonspecific (elevated with fibroids, endometriosis, PID)
Multivariate risk indices (e.g., OVA1, ROMA) help stratify indeterminate masses
Malignancy red flags: solid components, papillary projections, ascites, high color Doppler flow, bilaterality
management: Low-risk simple cyst: expectant management with repeat ultrasound (commonly around 6 months)
Indeterminate ultrasound findings: apply a validated risk-stratification tool before deciding on surgery
High-risk features (solid/papillary components, ascites, markedly elevated CA-125): refer to gynecologic oncology before any surgery
Premenopausal low-risk masses often resolve spontaneously; avoid unnecessary surgical intervention
When surgery is needed for a presumed-benign mass, favor a minimally invasive approach
Final diagnosis is pathologic, confirmed after surgical excision
citations: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 174, "Evaluation and Management of Adnexal Masses" (2016, reaffirmed 2024)

title: Pelvic Organ Prolapse and Urinary Incontinence
summary: POP-Q staging objectively grades prolapse, while a focused office evaluation distinguishes stress from urgency incontinence and guides a stepwise, conservative-to-surgical treatment plan.
key_points: POP-Q stages 0-4 are based on the leading prolapse edge relative to the hymen (stage 2 = within 1 cm of hymen)
A basic office evaluation (history, exam, cough stress test, post-void residual) diagnoses most incontinence without advanced testing
Stress incontinence: leakage with cough/exertion from urethral hypermobility or sphincter deficiency
Urgency incontinence: sudden urge-associated leakage, often with frequency, consistent with overactive bladder
Mixed incontinence is common; identify the predominant symptom to guide initial treatment
Post-void residual and urinalysis help exclude retention and infection as contributors
management: Prolapse first-line/conservative: pelvic floor physical therapy and vaginal pessary
Prolapse surgical repair reserved for symptomatic or pessary-refractory cases, tailored to the compartment involved
Stress incontinence first-line: pelvic floor muscle training; continence pessary/device as adjunct
Stress incontinence surgical: midurethral sling is the standard surgical option for refractory cases
Urgency incontinence/OAB first-line: bladder training, fluid/caffeine modification, pelvic floor therapy
Urgency incontinence second-line: antimuscarinic agents or a beta-3 agonist (mirabegron)
Refractory OAB: onabotulinumtoxinA bladder injection or sacral/tibial neuromodulation
citations: ACOG/AUGS Practice Bulletin No. 214, "Pelvic Organ Prolapse" (2019, reaffirmed 2024)
ACOG/AUGS Practice Bulletin No. 155, "Urinary Incontinence in Women" (2015, reaffirmed 2025)

title: Menopause and Hormone Therapy
summary: Menopause is a clinical diagnosis, and systemic hormone therapy remains the most effective option for vasomotor and genitourinary symptoms when started within the favorable risk window.
key_points: Menopause is diagnosed clinically: 12 months of amenorrhea without another cause, typically around age 51
Hormone therapy is the most effective treatment for vasomotor symptoms and genitourinary syndrome of menopause
Favorable benefit-risk "window of opportunity": starting HT at age <60 or within 10 years of menopause onset
Risk profile depends on formulation, dose, route, duration, and whether a progestogen is used
Contraindications: unexplained vaginal bleeding, active/history of breast or estrogen-sensitive cancer, prior VTE/stroke/MI, active liver disease
Transdermal estrogen carries lower VTE/stroke risk than oral formulations
Low-dose vaginal estrogen can be appropriate for genitourinary symptoms even with some systemic HT contraindications
management: Confirm diagnosis clinically; labs are rarely needed except to exclude other causes of symptoms
First line for moderate-severe vasomotor symptoms without contraindications: systemic estrogen, plus a progestogen if the uterus is present
Genitourinary syndrome of menopause alone: low-dose vaginal estrogen, vaginal DHEA, or oral ospemifene
Nonhormonal vasomotor options: SSRIs/SNRIs, gabapentin, or the NK3-receptor antagonist fezolinetant
Reassess risk-benefit periodically; use the lowest effective dose for the duration needed to meet goals
HT also prevents bone loss; consider bisphosphonates if HT is contraindicated and fracture risk is high
citations: NAMS (The Menopause Society), 2022 Hormone Therapy Position Statement
NAMS (The Menopause Society), 2023 Nonhormone Therapy Position Statement for Menopausal Vasomotor Symptoms

title: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS)
summary: PCOS is diagnosed by Rotterdam criteria after excluding mimics, and management combines lifestyle and metabolic screening with targeted therapy for menstrual, androgenic, and fertility symptoms.
key_points: Rotterdam criteria: 2 of 3 — oligo/anovulation, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound (or elevated AMH as a surrogate)
If irregular cycles and hyperandrogenism are both present, ultrasound/AMH is not required for diagnosis
Must exclude mimics: thyroid dysfunction, hyperprolactinemia, nonclassic congenital adrenal hyperplasia
Fasting lipid profile recommended at diagnosis for all patients with PCOS regardless of age or BMI
Glycemic screening (oral glucose tolerance test preferred) at baseline and every 1-3 years, especially before pregnancy
Chronic anovulation with unopposed estrogen raises endometrial hyperplasia risk
management: Lifestyle modification (diet and exercise) is foundational for metabolic and reproductive symptoms
Combined hormonal contraceptives are first line for menstrual irregularity and hyperandrogenism absent contraindications
Metformin for metabolic features or glucose intolerance, alone or with ovulation induction
Letrozole is the preferred first-line ovulation induction agent for infertility
Clomiphene citrate or gonadotropins as second-line/alternative ovulation induction
Cyclic progestin or a levonorgestrel IUD for endometrial protection if amenorrheic/anovulatory
Screen for and address mood disorders, obstructive sleep apnea, and cardiovascular risk factors
citations: 2023 International Evidence-Based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (ASRM/ESHRE co-sponsored)

title: Uterine Fibroids
summary: The FIGO PALM-COEIN system standardizes fibroid location for workup and planning, and treatment ranges from expectant management to uterine-sparing procedures or hysterectomy based on symptoms and fertility goals.
key_points: FIGO PALM-COEIN classifies fibroids by location: types 0-8, from submucosal (0-2) to subserosal (5-7) and other (8)
Submucosal fibroids are most strongly linked to heavy menstrual bleeding and infertility
Most fibroids are asymptomatic; workup is driven by symptoms (heavy bleeding, bulk symptoms, pain, infertility)
Transvaginal ultrasound is first-line imaging; saline infusion sonography or MRI helps map submucosal fibroids for surgical planning
Other PALM-COEIN causes of abnormal bleeding must be excluded before attributing symptoms to fibroids alone
Screen for anemia in patients with heavy menstrual bleeding
management: Asymptomatic fibroids: expectant management, no treatment needed
Medical first-line for heavy bleeding: levonorgestrel IUD or combined hormonal contraceptives
Short-term medical option: GnRH agonist/antagonist (with add-back) to reduce bleeding or shrink fibroids preoperatively
Uterine-sparing procedural options: uterine artery embolization, MRI-guided focused ultrasound, laparoscopic radiofrequency ablation
Uterine-sparing surgery: myomectomy (hysteroscopic for submucosal; laparoscopic/open for larger fibroids) preserves fertility
Hysterectomy is definitive treatment for those who have completed childbearing or failed conservative therapy
Tailor the choice to fibroid location/size, symptom type, and fertility desires
citations: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 228, "Management of Symptomatic Uterine Leiomyomas" (2021)
FIGO Leiomyoma Subclassification System, PALM-COEIN (adopted 2011, refined 2018)
